difficultyReason: Single-premise argument with one obvious gap. The doctor concludes the medication works because patients recovered, but assumes they would not have recovered without it.
stimulus: Cardiologist: All patients with heart arrhythmia who took the new medication recovered within two weeks. We can therefore conclude that the medication is effective.
questionStem: The cardiologist's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: patients with heart arrhythmia cannot recover on their own

choices.label: B
choices.text: the new medication is less expensive than existing treatments

choices.label: C
choices.text: heart arrhythmia is the most common cardiac condition

choices.label: D
choices.text: two weeks is a reasonable amount of time for recovery

choices.label: E
choices.text: all medications have some side effects

explanations.correct: The argument depends on the recovery being due to the medication. If patients could have recovered without it, then recovery alone does not prove effectiveness. So the argument must assume that recovery would not have occurred naturally.
explanations.A: Correct. Negating this (patients *could* recover on their own) undercuts the causal claim.
explanations.B: Cost is irrelevant to efficacy; this is out of scope.
explanations.C: Prevalence of the condition has no bearing on whether the medication works.
explanations.D: The reasonableness of the timeframe is not required for the efficacy claim.
explanations.E: The existence of side effects elsewhere does not affect this argument's validity.

difficultyReason: Direct logical gap: the speaker concludes a policy will lower emissions but assumes the policy actually creates the stated incentive.
stimulus: Environmental economist: The government's new carbon tax will lower industrial emissions because it makes polluting more expensive, and companies respond to financial incentives.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the economist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the carbon tax will not harm low-income workers

choices.label: B
choices.text: companies will view the carbon tax as a genuine financial disincentive to pollute

choices.label: C
choices.text: industrial pollution is the leading cause of climate change

choices.label: D
choices.text: no other country has ever implemented a carbon tax

choices.label: E
choices.text: the government has consulted with environmental scientists

explanations.correct: The economist's reasoning is: tax → financial disincentive → companies respond → lower emissions. This chain assumes companies will actually perceive and act on the tax as a disincentive. If they don't view it that way, the mechanism breaks.
explanations.A: Distributional fairness is a separate policy question; the efficacy of the tax does not depend on it.
explanations.B: Correct. Without this assumption, companies might ignore or discount the tax.
explanations.C: The argument is about reducing industrial emissions, not ranking climate causes.
explanations.D: Other countries' policies do not affect whether this tax works.
explanations.E: Consultation with scientists is not required for the tax to achieve its economic effect.

difficultyReason: One clear gap: the speaker infers quality from a single observable fact and assumes that fact reliably indicates quality.
stimulus: Art dealer: The newly discovered painting bears the artist's signature and was found in her estate. Therefore, it is an authentic work by her.
questionStem: The art dealer's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the artist never signed paintings that were not her own work

choices.label: B
choices.text: paintings found in an artist's estate are always valuable

choices.label: C
choices.text: the artist lived during the twentieth century

choices.label: D
choices.text: forgeries of the artist's work are rare in the market

choices.label: E
choices.text: the artist kept all her completed paintings in her estate

explanations.correct: The dealer uses signature + estate location as proof of authenticity. This only works if a genuine signature is not found on forgeries or unsigned works. Negating A (the artist *did* sign non-authentic works) would destroy the inference.
explanations.A: Correct. Without this, the signature proves nothing about authenticity.
explanations.B: Value is independent of whether the argument for authenticity succeeds.
explanations.C: The artist's era does not affect the validity of the signature-based inference.
explanations.D: Rarity of forgeries is not required; even one forgery with her signature would be enough to break the argument.
explanations.E: Whether she kept all paintings is irrelevant to whether this one is authentic.

difficultyReason: Clear causal gap: the speaker attributes a result to a specific cause but must assume that cause is the only operative factor.
stimulus: Linguist: Speakers of Language X struggle to distinguish the sounds /l/ and /r/. This is because Language X has no separate phonemes for these sounds. Therefore, language structure determines perception.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the linguist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Language X is more difficult to learn than English

choices.label: B
choices.text: the inability to distinguish /l/ and /r/ is not due to factors other than phonemic structure

choices.label: C
choices.text: all languages that lack a phonemic distinction are equally difficult

choices.label: D
choices.text: speakers of Language X never hear /l/ and /r/ distinguished in their environment

choices.label: E
choices.text: perception of sounds cannot be improved through training

explanations.correct: The argument infers that language structure (lack of phoneme distinction) causes the perceptual difficulty. This inference requires that no other cause—such as exposure, age of acquisition, or individual hearing variation—accounts for the difficulty.
explanations.A: Overall language difficulty is broader than this specific sound-perception claim.
explanations.B: Correct. If other factors caused the difficulty, structure wouldn't be the determining cause.
explanations.C: Relative difficulty across languages is not required for the causal claim.
explanations.D: Speakers of Language X may hear these sounds outside their language and still fail to distinguish them natively.
explanations.E: Whether training can improve perception later does not affect the current causal attribution.

difficultyReason: Single gap: the speaker uses absence of evidence as evidence of absence, assuming the absence is reliable.
stimulus: Historian: No documents from the medieval period mention a royal decree abolishing trade guilds. Therefore, no such decree was ever issued.
questionStem: The historian's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: medieval trade guilds were not very powerful

choices.label: B
choices.text: if such a decree had been issued, it would have been documented

choices.label: C
choices.text: most medieval documents have been preserved

choices.label: D
choices.text: trade guilds existed throughout the entire medieval period

choices.label: E
choices.text: the monarch had the authority to issue such a decree

explanations.correct: The argument treats the absence of documentary evidence as proof the decree never happened. This only holds if a real decree *would* have been documented. Negating B (the decree might not have been documented) lets the decree exist undocumented, so the argument collapses.
explanations.A: Guild power does not determine whether a decree would be documented.
explanations.B: Correct. Without this, the absence of documents proves nothing.
explanations.C: The assumption is narrower: only that a royal decree (if issued) would be documented, not all documents.
explanations.D: Whether guilds persisted is separate from whether a decree abolishing them occurred.
explanations.E: Formal authority to issue a decree is not required to argue whether it was issued.

difficultyReason: Straightforward causal inference with one necessary link: the speaker assumes that a measured property reflects what they claim.
stimulus: Psychologist: The study measured cortisol levels in participants before and after meditation. Cortisol levels dropped significantly. We can conclude that meditation reduces stress.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the psychologist's argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: cortisol is the only hormone affected by meditation

choices.label: B
choices.text: elevated cortisol levels are a reliable indicator of stress

choices.label: C
choices.text: participants in the study had never meditated before

choices.label: D
choices.text: meditation is more effective than prescription anxiolytics

choices.label: E
choices.text: cortisol levels should be measured in the morning

explanations.correct: The psychologist infers stress reduction from a drop in cortisol. This inference assumes that cortisol drop reflects stress reduction—i.e., that elevated cortisol indicates stress. Without this, a cortisol drop could be meaningless to the stress claim.
explanations.A: Other hormones need not be affected; only cortisol's relationship to stress matters.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument chains cortisol-drop to stress-reduction via this link.
explanations.C: Prior meditation history does not affect the current meditation→cortisol drop inference.
explanations.D: Comparative effectiveness versus other treatments is outside the argument's scope.
explanations.E: Measurement timing is not required for the causal claim itself.

difficultyReason: One clear assumption: the speaker uses a definition or category membership to make an inference and assumes that category assignment is correct.
stimulus: Legal scholar: The contract specifies that disputes will be resolved by arbitration. Therefore, the parties cannot bring a lawsuit in court.
questionStem: The scholar's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the parties did not intend to preserve their right to litigate

choices.label: B
choices.text: courts will enforce an arbitration clause by refusing to hear the case

choices.label: C
choices.text: the contract was signed by both parties simultaneously

choices.label: D
choices.text: arbitration is cheaper than litigation

choices.label: E
choices.text: there are no exceptions to the arbitration clause

explanations.correct: The argument infers that an arbitration clause bars court proceedings. This assumes courts will actually enforce the clause by dismissing lawsuits. Without this enforcement assumption, the clause could be unenforceable or ignored.
explanations.A: Intent is subsumed in the clause itself; the argument does not turn on what the parties internally intended.
explanations.B: Correct. The clause's existence alone does not bar litigation unless courts enforce it.
explanations.C: Timing of signing does not affect the clause's meaning or enforceability.
explanations.D: Cost considerations do not determine legal effect.
explanations.E: The argument does not require that the clause is absolute; even limited enforceability would support the conclusion that court suits are barred in most cases.

difficultyReason: Simple inference linking two observable facts; assumes the link is not coincidental.
stimulus: Technology analyst: After the company released version 3.0 of its software, user complaints about lag dropped by 50 percent. Therefore, version 3.0 fixed the lag problem.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the analyst's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: users did not stop using the software after the update

choices.label: B
choices.text: the drop in lag complaints was caused by the release of version 3.0, not by an unrelated change

choices.label: C
choices.text: version 2.0 had more features than version 3.0

choices.label: D
choices.text: the company hired more customer service representatives after the update

choices.label: E
choices.text: users prefer version 3.0 to all previous versions

explanations.correct: The analyst infers causation from temporal sequence: update → complaint drop. This requires that the drop was caused by the update, not by coincidence or some other intervening event (e.g., users switching to a different app, change in reporting platform). Negating B (the drop was due to something else) breaks the causal inference.
explanations.A: User retention is not directly required; the argument concerns complaint reduction.
explanations.B: Correct. Without this, the timing is merely coincidental.
explanations.C: Feature parity between versions does not affect the lag-fix inference.
explanations.D: Customer service staffing does not explain a technical lag fix.
explanations.E: User preference ranking is separate from whether the lag problem was fixed.

difficultyReason: One clear gap: the speaker categorizes something and assumes the category membership has a stated implication.
stimulus: Ethics instructor: All cases of deception that harm others are morally wrong. This business practice is a case of deception that harms consumers. Therefore, this business practice is morally wrong.
questionStem: The instructor's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: the business knew the practice would harm consumers

choices.label: B
choices.text: consumers are more vulnerable than other groups

choices.label: C
choices.text: there are no other moral considerations that override the wrongness

choices.label: D
choices.text: the practice does indeed harm consumers

choices.label: E
choices.text: businesses are held to a higher ethical standard than individuals

explanations.correct: The instructor uses categorical logic: if it's deception-that-harms, then it's morally wrong. The conclusion requires that the premise is true—i.e., that the practice actually does harm consumers. If it doesn't harm them, the major premise doesn't apply.
explanations.A: Intent (knowledge) is not required; only that harm actually occurs.
explanations.B: Vulnerability ranking is irrelevant to the moral-wrongness categorization.
explanations.C: The argument does not address competing moral considerations; necessity doesn't extend to it.
explanations.D: Correct. Without this factual premise, the deception doesn't fall under the 'harms-others' category.
explanations.E: Standard of care for businesses vs. individuals is not part of the logical structure.

difficultyReason: Direct causal inference: the speaker links two phenomena and assumes one did not occur without the other.
stimulus: Nutritionist: The study tracked two identical groups of office workers over six months. Group A was given access to a standing desk, while Group B continued using traditional chairs. Group A reported significantly less back pain. Therefore, standing desks reduce back pain.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the nutritionist's argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: standing desks are not more expensive than traditional desks

choices.label: B
choices.text: back pain in Group B was not caused by other workplace factors unrelated to desk type

choices.label: C
choices.text: the two groups had no prior differences in back pain history

choices.label: D
choices.text: standing desks are used by most office workers today

choices.label: E
choices.text: sitting in a chair is the primary cause of all back pain

explanations.correct: The argument compares two groups and attributes the difference in back pain outcomes to the desk type. For this comparison to be valid, the groups must have been equivalent at the start. If Group A already had less back pain history, the desk type is not the cause of the observed difference.
explanations.A: Cost does not affect the causal efficacy of the desks.
explanations.B: Other workplace factors in Group B are addressed by the group comparison structure; the assumption concerns initial equivalence, not confounds within groups.
explanations.C: Correct. A controlled experiment (identical groups) requires identical starting conditions.
explanations.D: Current usage rates do not affect the causal inference from the study.
explanations.E: The argument claims desks reduce pain, not that sitting causes all back pain.
